docs.title: Crosswork CNC Hands-on
docs.text: This is the operator lab for Cisco Crosswork Network Controller (CNC) 7.2.1-SP. You will use a dedicated controller and a Cisco Modeling Labs (CML) topology.

docs.title: How to read each chapter
docs.text: Each chapter has an objective, the clicks, the result you should see, and a short "done when" list. Router work in this lab is show output. Configuration changes go through CNC, and only in the chapters that say so.

docs.title: View this guide
docs.text:
From this folder, with the existing virtual environment:

source venv/bin/activate
mkdocs serve

Open the local URL MkDocs prints. mkdocs build writes the static site under site/.

docs.title: 1. Preparation
docs.text:
Time: 20 minutes, most of it waiting.

Objective: Leave maintenance mode, start the CML lab, and log in to a controller that is ready for work.

Instructor

Maintenance mode shuts the applications down gracefully, and bringing them back takes several minutes.

docs.title: 1.1 Disable maintenance mode
docs.text:
Maintenance mode is how CNC stops itself cleanly for a reboot, a backup, or a restore. After a reboot that began in maintenance mode, the cluster comes back in maintenance mode and waits for the slider to be turned off.

  1. Sign in to the dCloud.

  2. Access Ubuntu2204-1T-Desktop, run Firefox on the Desktop and open CNC UI (username and password are shared in the session)

    https://[2001:db8:134::200]:30603

  3. Go to Administration > Settings > System Settings > Maintenance Mode.

  4. If a popup already offers to turn maintenance mode off, accept it.

  5. If the Maintenance slider is On, drag it to Off and confirm.

  6. Wait. The applications need several minutes.

Result: The maintenance slider stays Off, the UI loads the normal home page.

docs.title: 1.2 Start the CML lab
docs.text:
1. Open another tab on Firefox and click "CML2 for XR" in the bookmark.
  2. Start "5-nodes_L3VPN 8201-32FH 25.3.1-ipv6" scenario
  3. Open another tab on Firefox and click "CML2 for PCE" in the bookmark.
  4. Start "xrv9k-25.4.1-pce-for-CNC7.2-ipv6" scenario

Result: The lab is booted. CNC can reach the devices after the providers and the Data Gateway are healthy. You confirm that reachability in the next chapter.

Result: You are in the UI as yourself, and the controller is in normal operating mode.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• Maintenance mode is Off.
  • Log in to CNC
  • The CML labs are booted.

docs.title: 2. CNC management
docs.text:
Time: 40 minutes.

Objective: Decide whether the platform is healthy enough for topology, inventory, traffic engineering, and service provisioning. You are reading the system, not rebuilding it.

The three dependencies for the rest of the lab:

Later work Depends on Topology and SR policies SR-PCE provider, BGP-LS and PCEP from the routers Inventory, alarms, interface utilization Crosswork Data Gateway collection L3VPN provisioning NSO provider, devices in sync

docs.title: 2.1 Application health
docs.text:
1. Go to Administration > Crosswork Manager.
  2. Open the cluster or application view the page offers.
  3. Find these applications and read the state next to each one:
    • Platform infrastructure
    • Optimization Engine
    • Active Topology
    • Element Management Functions / Device Lifecycle Management
    • Data Gateway related services
  4. A state of Running or Healthy is what you want before chapter 3. Degraded and Down belong on the checkpoint page.

Result: You can name the applications this lab uses and their states.

Leave restart, node drain, and maintenance controls untouched. You already finished maintenance mode in chapter 1.

docs.title: 2.2 Providers
docs.text:
CNC learns the routed topology from SR-PCE. CNC provisions services through NSO. Both are providers.

  1. Go to Administration > Manage Provider Access.
  2. Find the SR-PCE provider. Read its reachability and the protocol state. You want the provider reachable, with the topology feed up.
  3. Find the NSO provider. Read its reachability. You want NSO reachable.
  4. Open the provider detail far enough to see the credential profile name. The profile is a pointer. The password stays in the profile store.

Result: SR-PCE and NSO are both reachable. If either is down, stop and use the checkpoint page before chapter 5 or chapter 6. Chapters 3 and 4 can still teach the screens.

docs.title: 2.3 Data Gateway
docs.text:
Interface counters, inventory detail, syslog, and SNMP traps arrive through a Crosswork Data Gateway (CDG). LCM in chapter 7 reads interface utilization from this collection, through SNMP.

  1. Go to Administration > Data Gateway Management, or the Data Gateway page linked from Crosswork Manager.
  2. Confirm the gateway is enrolled and the pool is up.
  3. Open one attached device and confirm a data gateway is mapped to it. A device with no gateway mapping has no inventory refresh and no interface counters.
  4. If a collection job or destination is listed, read its status. Healthy collection is the bar.

Result: You can point at the gateway that will feed alarms, inventory, and utilization.

docs.title: 2.4 What you leave alone
docs.text:
Credential profiles, AAA, certificates, backup jobs, and licensing are visible from Administration and from Device Management > Credential Profiles. Open a profile only if a device is unreachable and the instructor asks you to compare the profile name. Editing a profile on a shared controller locks every other seat out of that device.

Backup and restore put the cluster into maintenance mode. They are out of scope for this session.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• Optimization Engine, Active Topology, and element management are Running or Healthy.
  • The SR-PCE provider is reachable.
  • The NSO provider is reachable.
  • A Data Gateway is enrolled and mapped to the lab devices.

docs.title: 3. Active Topology (CAT)
docs.text:
Time: 45 minutes.

Objective: Use Crosswork Active Topology to answer where a device sits, how it is connected, and which layer you are looking at.

Active Topology is the map. Optimization Engine supplies the traffic-engineering view on top of the same topology. You will switch between those views so the two products stay distinct in your notes.

docs.title: 3.1 Open the map
docs.text:
1. From the main menu, open Topology.
  2. Wait for the devices from the CML lab to appear. A topology that stays empty usually means the SR-PCE provider is up and BGP-LS is down, or the CML nodes are still booting. Check chapter 2 and the checkpoint page.
  3. Switch between the logical map and the geographical map if both are offered. The logical map is the one you will use for the rest of the day.
  4. Zoom to the two provider edges named on your lab-values sheet. Those are the headend and the endpoint for chapters 5 and 6.

Result: You can find both PEs and at least one path between them.

docs.title: 3.2 Read a device and a link
docs.text:
1. Select the headend. Open the details panel.
  2. Record the hostname, the management address, and the reachability state.
  3. Select a core link that sits on a path between the headend and the endpoint.
  4. In the link details, record:
    • IGP metric
    • TE metric, if one is shown
    • Interface names on each side
    • Utilization, if a value is shown
    • Adjacency SID or SRv6 adjacency information, if the link shows it
  5. Say out loud which value a PCE would minimize if the objective was IGP metric, and which value it would minimize if the objective was TE metric.

Utilization on a CML link is often 0%. Write down the number you actually see. Chapter 7 uses it.

Result: One device record and one link record in your notes.

docs.title: 3.3 Layers and filters
docs.text:
The map can show more than one underlay. PTA's core work is segment routing, with SRv6 as the policy type when the whiteboard says so.

  1. Open the layer or protocol selector.
  2. Turn on the IGP layer and confirm the links you care about are still there.
  3. Turn on the SR-MPLS or SRv6 layer that matches the whiteboard. Adjacency and prefix SID information belongs to this layer.
  4. If a Flex-Algo layer is present, note the algorithm id and leave it. Flex-Algo is a map fact in this lab, not a configuration task.
  5. Apply a filter or device group that shows only the lab core, if a group already exists. Creating a new group is optional and is an instructor choice on a shared map.

Result: You can turn the TE layer on and still recognize the same two PEs.

docs.title: 3.4 Dashboard tiles
docs.text:
1. Return to the home page or the topology dashboard.
  2. Read the tiles that summarize device reachability, link state, and policy count.
  3. If a tile shows zero SR policies, that is acceptable before chapter 5. Write the number down so you can compare it after you create a PCE-initiated policy.

Result: You have a baseline count of policies and of reachable devices.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• Both lab PEs are on the map and reachable.
  • You recorded metric and utilization for one core link.
  • You can show the IGP layer and the segment-routing layer.
  • You know the baseline SR policy count.

docs.title: 4. Element management (EMF)
docs.text:
Time: 60 minutes.

Objective: Use the CNC 7.1 element-management functions to read inventory, archived configuration, a configuration template, alarms, events, and performance. Deploy nothing from this chapter.

Element Management Functions in CNC 7.1 cover device onboarding, inventory, faults, metrics, software images, configuration backup, and configuration templates. ZTP is part of the same lifecycle guide. You will tour ZTP in chapter 8 so this hour stays on "what is on the device today."

docs.title: 4.1 Network devices and inventory
docs.text:
1. Go to Device Management > Network Devices.
  2. Find the headend. Read operational state, reachability, and the credential profile name.
  3. Confirm a Data Gateway is associated with the device. Chapter 2 introduced that mapping. This is where a missing mapping shows up as a device you cannot refresh.
  4. Go to Device Management > Network Inventory.
  5. Filter to the headend hostname or product family.
  6. Open the chassis, one route processor or line card, and one pluggable if the inventory has them.
  7. Open the alarm summary on that inventory row. You will come back to the full alarm list in section 4.4.

Result: You can walk from a hostname to a chassis and a module, and you know whether the device is reachable.

A device that stays unreachable for the whole session needs the checkpoint page: credentials, routing to the management address, and CML node state. Give it a few minutes after the lab boots before you call it failed.

docs.title: 4.2 Configuration backup
docs.text:
CNC can archive device configuration, compare two archives, and restore. This lab uses the archive as a reader.

  1. Go to Device Management > Configuration Backup and Restore.
  2. Find the headend.
  3. Open the latest archived configuration and identify the hostname and the segment-routing or BGP section the instructor points out.
  4. If two archives exist, open the compare view and name one difference, or state that the two archives match.
  5. Leave Schedule backup and Restore unused.

Result: You have seen a real archived configuration for the headend and you know where a later change would show up.

Automatic backup on configuration change, when it is enabled under Device Management > Configuration Preferences, is what makes this archive useful after chapter 6. Read the preference. Leave the values as you found them.

docs.title: 4.3 Configuration templates
docs.text:
Device templates under Device Management are parameterized CLI (Apache Velocity template language). They are for repeating underlay or day-1 configuration across similar devices. They are a different store from the NSO L2VPN and L3VPN function-pack templates that chapter 6 uses.

  1. Go to Device Management > Configuration Templates.
  2. Open one existing template. Read the device types it targets and one variable it expects.
  3. Open Jobs only if a previous job is listed, and read its status.
  4. Close the template. Leave Create Template and every deploy action unused.

Result: You can explain the difference between this template library and the service template NSO applies when you provision an L3VPN.

Deploying a template from this screen writes CLI to live routers. That write is out of scope for a shared class.

docs.title: 4.4 Alarms and events
docs.text:
1. Go to Alerts > Alarms and Events.
  2. Stay on Alarms. Use the category list to see system, network, and device alarms as separate sets.
  3. Filter to the headend if the filter allows it.
  4. If an alarm is present, record severity, source, and whether it is acknowledged. Leave acknowledge, clear, and annotate unused unless the instructor gives you a lab alarm of your own.
  5. Switch Show from Alarms to Events.
  6. Read the newest event. An event is a moment in time. An alarm remains until it clears. Use one sentence to put the event you found into one of those two buckets.

Result: You can open both views and you did not clear someone else's alarm.

An empty alarm list is a valid result on a healthy CML lab. Write "no active device alarms" and move on.

docs.title: 4.5 Performance
docs.text:
Link colors on the topology map come from interface utilization collected for Optimization Engine. Element management adds polling policies and device-level metrics.

  1. Go to Device Management > Performance Policies, or the performance page under Device Management on your build.
  2. Open one existing policy. Read which devices or groups it covers, how often it polls, and which threshold raises an alarm.
  3. Return to the headend in Network Inventory or Network Devices and open the metrics or interface view. Compare one interface counter with the utilization you wrote down in chapter 3.
  4. Leave the policy inactive/active switch as you found it. A new polling policy on every seat multiplies SNMP load on the lab.

Result: You can say where a threshold is defined, and you can point at one live counter.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• The headend is in Network Devices and in Network Inventory.
  • You opened an archived configuration and a device template, and you deployed neither.
  • You opened Alarms and Events.
  • You can point at the polling policy that would raise a threshold alarm.

docs.title: 5. Segment Routing and Traffic Engineering
docs.text:
Time: 75 minutes.

Objective: Explain a PCC-initiated policy that the headend already owns, then create one PCE-initiated SR policy from CNC with your own name and color.

Use the policy type on the whiteboard. For this PTA lab that type is SRv6 when the core is SRv6, and SR-MPLS when the core is SR-MPLS. The CNC pages are the same shape. Pick the tab that matches the whiteboard and stay on it.

docs.title: 5.1 Words you need
docs.text: Term Meaning in this lab PCC The headend router. It may ask SR-PCE for a path, and it can own a policy that was configured on the router. PCE SR-PCE. It computes paths and can instantiate a policy on a headend through PCEP. PCC-initiated The policy configuration lives on the headend. CNC learns the policy from SR-PCE and draws it. PCE-initiated You create the policy in CNC. SR-PCE pushes it to the headend. The headend shows it as delegated to the PCE. Color A number that identifies the intent. Steering in chapter 6 binds a VPN to a color. Candidate path One way to reach the endpoint. Preference chooses among candidate paths.

docs.title: 5.2 Find the PCC-initiated policy
docs.text:
The instructor prepares one PCC-initiated policy before class, on the headend, with a color outside the 200 + seat range. You do not type that router configuration.

  1. Go to Services & Traffic Engineering > Traffic Engineering.
  2. Open the SRv6 or SR-MPLS tab named on the whiteboard.
  3. Filter or sort the policy table until you find the PCC-initiated policy. The initiation column says PCC.
  4. Record headend, endpoint, color, preference, and the active candidate path.
  5. Select the policy and show it on the map. Name two hops on the drawn path.
  6. If the table has no PCC row, say so. The rest of this chapter still works. The live create is the PCE-initiated policy. Tell the instructor the prepared PCC policy is missing.

Result: You can point at a policy the router owns, or you have recorded that the prepared policy is absent.

On the headend console, if the instructor opens one, these commands support the same story. Read them. Leave configuration mode.

show segment-routing traffic-eng policy
show segment-routing traffic-eng pcc ipv4 peer

On an IPv6-only SRv6 headend the peer command may be the IPv6 form:

show segment-routing traffic-eng pcc ipv6 peer

Use the form the instructor shows. In the output, find the color of the PCC policy and the PCE peer address.

docs.title: 5.3 Create a PCE-initiated policy
docs.text:
Your policy name is pta-pce-seat-<seat>. Your color is 200 + seat. Two seats that reuse a color will fight over steering in chapter 6.

  1. Stay on Services & Traffic Engineering > Traffic Engineering, on the same SRv6 or SR-MPLS tab.
  2. Start the create action and choose PCE-initiated.
  3. Set:
    • Name: pta-pce-seat-<seat>
    • Headend: the headend from your lab-values sheet
    • Endpoint: the endpoint from your lab-values sheet
    • Color: 200 + seat
    • Optimization objective: IGP metric, unless the instructor writes a different objective
  4. Leave bandwidth, affinity, and disjoint constraints empty unless the instructor adds one constraint for the whole room.
  5. Preview the path. You want a path that passes through the core, from your headend to your endpoint.
  6. If the preview is empty, stop. An empty preview means SR-PCE has no topology or no SID reachability. Use the checkpoint page. Committing an empty path teaches the wrong lesson.
  7. When the preview shows a path, provision the policy.
  8. Return to the policy table. Your row shows initiation PCE, your color, and an operational state that is up.
  9. Select the row and display the path on the map.

Result: A PCE-initiated policy exists for your seat, and the map draws it.

docs.title: 5.4 Confirm on the headend
docs.text:
Ask the instructor for a console on the headend, or watch the instructor's console.

show segment-routing traffic-eng policy

Find pta-pce-seat-<seat>. In the same output, the PCC-initiated policy is still present. The difference is ownership: one policy is configured on the router, and the other was instantiated by the PCE.

If your policy is missing on the router and present in CNC as down, the usual causes are a PCEP session that is down, a color conflict, or a headend that cannot place the SIDs. Stay with the checkpoint page. Delete only your own down policy, and only when the instructor agrees.

docs.title: 5.5 Clean-up rule
docs.text: Keep this policy until chapter 6 has steered a VPN onto its color. At the end of the day, delete only pta-pce-seat-<seat>. Leave the PCC-initiated policy in place for the next session.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• You can say who owns the PCC-initiated policy and who owns yours.
  • Your PCE-initiated policy is up, with your color, and it is drawn on the map.
  • You saw both policies in show segment-routing traffic-eng policy, or you have a written reason the headend console was unavailable.

docs.title: 6. Intent-based L3VPN provisioning
docs.text:
Time: 75 minutes.

Objective: Create one L3VPN from CNC. NSO renders the device configuration from the service model and the function-pack template. Steer the VPN onto the PCE-initiated policy from chapter 5.

The UI path is Services & Traffic Engineering > Provisioning (NSO). CNC 7.1 provisions IETF L3VPN network models through NSO. You fill in the service intent. You do not paste CLI, and you do not edit the XML template on the NSO server.

docs.title: 6.1 What you are about to commit
docs.text:
Each seat creates a different service:

Field Value Service name PTA-L3-SEAT-<seat> Endpoints the two PEs on your lab-values sheet, using the attachment points the instructor assigns Route distinguisher and route targets the pair on the whiteboard for your seat Steering preferred path, bound to color 200 + seat Transport the same SRv6 or SR-MPLS type you used in chapter 5

Preferred path is the steering method for this lab because the map can show the VPN sitting on the policy you just created. On-demand next hop (ODN) is the other method: the headend builds a path when it receives a route with that color. Read the ODN choice in the form so you recognize it, then select preferred path.

If the PTA service profile on this controller exposes only one steering knob, use the one the instructor names. Record which one you used.

docs.title: 6.2 Create the service
docs.text:
1. Go to Services & Traffic Engineering > Provisioning (NSO).
  2. Open the L3VPN service type.
  3. Create a service named PTA-L3-SEAT-<seat>.
  4. Select the instance profile or VPN profile the instructor named. That profile points at the NSO L3VPN template. You are choosing it, not editing it.
  5. Enter the route distinguisher and route targets for your seat.
  6. Add the two endpoints. For each endpoint set the device, the attachment circuit or interface, and the PE-CE routing the instructor specified. A lab that uses a static route on one side and BGP on the other is still one L3VPN. Follow the whiteboard.
  7. Set the underlay transport to the policy type from chapter 5.
  8. Set steering to preferred path and select color 200 + seat, or select the policy pta-pce-seat-<seat> if the form asks for a policy name.
  9. Run Dry run before Commit. Read the preview far enough to see your service name, your two endpoints, and the color. A preview that names another seat's VPN is the wrong form. Close it and start again from your own service name.
  10. Commit.
  11. Open the service and read the sync state. In sync means NSO and the devices agree. Out of sync belongs on the checkpoint page before you troubleshoot the VPN itself.

Result: PTA-L3-SEAT-<seat> is committed and in sync.

docs.title: 6.3 See it on the map
docs.text:
1. Open Services & Traffic Engineering > VPN Services, or the service overlay the provisioning page links to.
  2. Select your VPN.
  3. Show the service path and the underlay policy together.
  4. Confirm the underlay is pta-pce-seat-<seat>, or a path whose color is 200 + seat.

Result: You can show a neighbour the service and the SR policy it rides.

docs.title: 6.4 Read the effect on the PE
docs.text:
On the headend, with the instructor's console:

show bgp vpnv4 unicast summary
show bgp vpnv6 unicast summary

Use the address family this lab actually runs. PTA's IPv6 core still may carry an IPv4 VPN, an IPv6 VPN, or both. The whiteboard says which summary command should show your VRF.

Then:

show vrf
show segment-routing traffic-eng policy

You want the VRF for PTA-L3-SEAT-<seat> and the same PCE-initiated policy as chapter 5. Leave configuration mode.

docs.title: 6.5 Templates, stated once
docs.text: The XML templates in the NSO L3VPN function pack are what turned your form into CLI. Device Management templates from chapter 4 did not. If a dry run fails with a template or profile error, the profile name is the thing to check. Editing the package on the NSO server is an instructor action outside this class.

docs.title: 6.6 Clean-up rule
docs.text: Keep your VPN until you have shown it on the map. At the end of the day, delete PTA-L3-SEAT-<seat> from the provisioning page, then delete your PCE-initiated policy. Deleting the policy first, while the VPN still prefers it, leaves the service with nowhere to steer. Order is VPN, then policy.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• Dry run showed your service name, your endpoints, and your color.
  • The service is in sync.
  • The VPN overlay draws your service on your PCE-initiated policy.
  • You can say which template store rendered the CLI.

docs.title: 7. Closed-loop congestion mitigation
docs.text:
Time: 45 minutes.

Objective: Read Local Congestion Mitigation (LCM) on CNC 7.1, explain the closed loop, and leave the shared network in Manual mode.

docs.title: 7.1 Lab decision
docs.text:
LCM is a real Optimization Engine feature in CNC 7.1, and it is the right exercise for this chapter. It looks for congestion on a timer, estimates traffic that can be moved off a hot interface, and recommends tactical traffic-engineering (TTE) SR policies around that interface. In Manual mode an operator previews the recommendation and then commits it. SR-PCE deploys the tactical policies. When the interface cools, LCM recommends removal.

LCM sees congestion through SNMP interface counters collected by the Data Gateway. It also needs a discovered IGP domain (the BGP-LS link-state instance-id), an alternate local path, and a tactical color that no other policy uses.

A CML topology often reports 0% utilization, because the links carry no traffic. LCM then has nothing to mitigate. That outcome still completes this chapter. Record the utilization and the threshold, and explain why the operational dashboard has no recommendation.

Instructor

Keep the domain in Manual mode. Automated mode deploys tactical policies without a human commit, and in later releases it also requires a fully gRPC-compliant domain. Students do not change the mode.

Commit a recommendation only when one domain shows a real recommendation and you want the room to see a single deploy. Use the reserved tactical color. Students do not click Commit all.

If you want a live PCE action and every interface is idle, use Bandwidth on Demand as a demonstration. BWoD asks for a path with a bandwidth number. It does not need a hot link. It is a different feature. Show it from the instructor console, and keep the student exercise on the LCM screens.

docs.title: 7.2 Open the domain
docs.text:
1. Go to Services & Traffic Engineering > Local Congestion Mitigation.
  2. Read the domain card. The domain id comes from the IGP link-state instance-id advertised in BGP-LS.
  3. Record:
    • LCM status (enabled or not)
    • Operation mode
    • Urgency
    • The description, which defaults to "LCM Startup Config" on a fresh configuration
  4. If the card says the domain is not configured, stop and let the instructor open Configure. The room uses one LCM configuration.

Result: You know the domain id and the operation mode. The mode you want to see is Manual.

docs.title: 7.3 Read the thresholds and the loop
docs.text:
1. Open Interface Thresholds. Find one core interface you recorded in chapter 3. Read its utilization threshold.
  2. Compare that threshold with the utilization you wrote down from the topology map. Say which side of the threshold the interface is on.
  3. Open Configuration. Read the congestion check interval, the optimization objective, and the operation mode. Leave every field as you found it.
  4. Walk the loop in your own words:
    • CDG polls interface counters with SNMP.
    • LCM compares utilization with the interface threshold on the check interval.
    • A hot interface produces a TTE SR policy recommendation that stays local to that hop.
    • In Manual mode the recommendation waits on the operational dashboard.
    • Commit sends the tactical policy through SR-PCE.
    • A later check recommends deletion when the interface is under the threshold again.

Result: You can teach the loop from the screens, with your own utilization number in the story.

docs.title: 7.4 Recommendations
docs.text:
1. Open the Operational Dashboard for the domain. Use the "Recommendations available" link when the card shows it.
  2. If a recommendation is listed, read urgency and the interfaces it would bypass. Preview it on the map. Then stop. The instructor commits, or nobody commits.
  3. If the dashboard is empty, write the sentence: "No recommendation, utilization is below the threshold." Include the two numbers.
  4. Open Operational History if it has rows from an earlier demo, and read one commit or one removal. History is part of the product even when this hour adds no new row.

Result: You have either previewed one recommendation or recorded why none exists.

docs.title: 7.5 What you leave alone
docs.text:
• The operation-mode control stays on Manual.
  • Commit all stays with the instructor.
  • The tactical color stays the reserved color, and it stays off your chapter 5 policy.
  • Per-interface threshold edits are an instructor tool for a demo. A room full of lowered thresholds creates a pile of recommendations against empty CML links.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• You can open the LCM domain, the thresholds, and the configuration.
  • You compared one interface's utilization with its threshold.
  • You can describe what a commit would deploy, and you did not deploy it yourself.
  • You know BWoD is the instructor's fallback when the lab has no congestion to show.

docs.title: 8. Lifecycle management and ZTP
docs.text:
Time: 20 minutes.

Objective: Walk the Zero Touch Provisioning screens so you can recognize images, configuration files, serial numbers, profiles, and devices. Leave every router in its current boot state.

CNC 7.1 puts ZTP under element management: Device Management > Zero Touch Provisioning. Classic ZTP uses DHCP and HTTP so a new router can pull an image and a configuration. Secure ZTP (RFC 8572) adds ownership vouchers and a signed exchange. This controller may show both. The PTA lab routers are already onboarded through the normal device inventory. They are the wrong devices to reload into ZTP during class.

docs.title: 8.1 Tour
docs.text:
Work down this list. Open each page, read the columns, and close it.

  1. Device Management > Software Management. This is the image and SMU store. Read one image name and the platform family, if any file is present. Upload nothing.
  2. Device Management > Zero Touch Provisioning > Configuration files. These are ZTP day-0 scripts, with replaceable parameters. They are a third store, different from Device Management templates and from NSO service templates. Open one file if it exists and find a single placeholder. Download the sample XR script only if the instructor wants the room to see the comments. Upload nothing.
  3. Device Management > Zero Touch Provisioning > Serial Numbers & Ownership. A device enters ZTP when its serial number is known here. Read the columns. Add no serial and import no CSV.
  4. Device Management > Credential Profiles. ZTP devices need a profile too. You already know this page from chapter 2. Confirm the lab profile is still the one you saw. Edit nothing.
  5. Device Management > Zero Touch Provisioning > ZTP profiles. A profile binds an image, a configuration file, and a device family. Open one profile tile if the lab has one. Create none.
  6. Device Management > Zero Touch Provisioning > Devices. This list is ZTP state, which is separate from Network Devices. If it is empty, the lab simply has no ZTP job in progress. That is the expected classroom state.

Result: You can name the six pages and say which object each one holds.

docs.title: 8.2 The workflow you are not running
docs.text:
Say this sequence back to the instructor, from the screens you just opened:

  1. The image is in Software Management.
  2. The day-0 configuration file is in the ZTP configuration store.
  3. The serial number is loaded, with an ownership voucher when the flow is Secure ZTP.
  4. A credential profile exists.
  5. A ZTP profile ties the image and the configuration to a device family.
  6. A device row tracks state from boot to onboarded.
  7. DHCP, or the secure ZTP bootstrap, points the hardware at this controller. After onboarding, the device also appears under Device Management > Network Devices.

The home page dashboard can show a ZTP status tile while a job runs. You may look for the tile. An absent tile means no active job.

docs.title: 8.3 Why this stays a tour
docs.text:
A real ZTP run reloads a device, depends on DHCP options or a secure bootstrap, and consumes a serial number. CML guests in this topology are already part of the IGP. Reloading one of them removes it from the map for every seat. Image upload and serial import are the same class of shared change.

Software image management for an already-managed router (upgrade and SMU) lives next to ZTP under Device Management > Software Management. Recognize the page. Start no upgrade.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• You visited Software Management, ZTP configuration files, serial numbers, ZTP profiles, and ZTP devices.
  • You can separate those objects from a Device Management template and from an NSO service template.
  • No image, serial, profile, or device row was created by your seat.

docs.title: 9. Proactive assurance and the MCP server
docs.text:
Time: 40 minutes.

Objective: See where CNC monitors service and device health, then ask the lab assistant one question that it can answer from a live Crosswork tool. You decide what to do with the answer.

docs.title: 9.1 Assurance on the controller
docs.text:
You already used device alarms, events, and performance policies in chapter 4. Two more CNC 7.1 applications sit above that, when they are installed on this cluster:

Application What an operator uses it for Service Health A service-level view of the L2VPN and L3VPN you provisioned, with symptoms against the rules the operator enabled Health Insights KPI monitoring and alerts driven by logic the operator attached to devices
  1. From the main menu or the application list, open Service Health if it is installed.
  2. Find PTA-L3-SEAT-<seat> if the service view has reached it. Read the health state and one symptom or rule name. If your service is absent, the collector has not scored it yet. Note the time and continue. Scoring can lag a new provision.
  3. Open Health Insights only if it is installed. Read one existing KPI profile. Enable no new KPI. A new profile on a shared cluster adds collection for every seat.
  4. If either application is missing from this single-VM lab, record "not installed" and continue with section 9.2. The MCP exercise is the required part of this chapter.

Result: You know whether service health is scoring your VPN, and you left KPI enablement unchanged.

docs.title: 9.2 The assistant and MCP
docs.text:
The lab assistant is a chat page. When you ask a question, the assistant may call tools on an MCP server. That server is what talks to Crosswork. The tools listed in the assistant sidebar are the only live data the assistant can fetch. Anything else in the reply is explanation, and you treat it as explanation until you confirm it in the CNC UI.

The instructor starts the assistant and the MCP server before this chapter. You receive the assistant URL on the whiteboard. You do not receive, and you do not type, the controller password, an API token, or a client secret. Those stay in the instructor's configuration outside this guide.

  1. Open the assistant URL.
  2. Read the backend status in the sidebar. Continue when it is online.
  3. Read the tool list. Find the tool whose description is the inventory node count. That is the live tool for this lab.
  4. If the sidebar also lists session or ticket tools, leave them unused. This chapter does not delete sessions and does not change the controller.

Result: The assistant is online and you can name the inventory tool.

docs.title: 9.3 One live question
docs.text:
In the chat, ask:

How many nodes are in the Crosswork inventory?

Wait for the reply. Open the tool-call detail the UI shows for that turn.

Check all of the following:

  • The assistant called the inventory count tool.
  • The reply contains a number.
  • You can find a matching count under Device Management > Network Devices or Network Inventory. The two screens group equipment differently, so the numbers may differ by what each one counts. Write both numbers and one sentence on the difference you see. If they match, write that they match.

If the tool call fails, the useful symptom is the error text, not a second guess from the model. A failure here usually means the assistant cannot authenticate to CNC or cannot reach the UI address. That is an instructor fix. Your earlier chapters already showed you the same inventory with your own login.

Result: A number from the tool, compared with the number you read in Device Management.

docs.title: 9.4 Remediation stays with you
docs.text:
Ask a second question that does not require a write tool:

The inventory count is <the number you just verified>.
The CML lab should have <the node count on the whiteboard> routers.
What should an operator check first in Crosswork?

A useful answer names checks you already know how to open:

  • Reachability on Device Management > Network Devices
  • The credential profile on that device
  • Data Gateway mapping
  • SR-PCE and NSO provider status
  • Active alarms for that hostname

Take one check the assistant named, open that CNC page, and confirm or contradict the suggestion with the screen. The screen wins. The assistant does not commit, delete, or provision.

That is the remediation pattern for this lab: the assistant reads, the assistant suggests, the operator verifies, the operator changes the network only through the chapters that allow a commit.

docs.title: 9.5 What you leave out of the chat
docs.text:
• Passwords, tokens, ticket ids, and certificate contents
  • A request to delete a session, a policy, a VPN, or a device
  • Configuration text copied from another seat's dry run

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• You know whether Service Health and Health Insights are installed.
  • The assistant answered the inventory question with a tool call.
  • You compared that number with Device Management.
  • You verified one suggested check on a CNC screen.

docs.title: Checkpoints
docs.text: Use this page when a chapter's expected result does not appear. Fix the first row that matches, then return to the chapter. One person applies a shared fix. Everyone else waits.

docs.title: Maintenance and login
docs.text: What you see What to check The UI never finishes loading after the slider moves Maintenance restart takes several minutes. Wait. If a popup asks to turn maintenance off, the instructor accepts it once. Applications stay down after maintenance is Off CNC 7.1: turn Maintenance On, wait until the mode is fully on, then turn it Off. Path: Administration > Settings > System Settings > Maintenance Mode. Certificate warning Confirm the hostname is the whiteboard URL, then use the lab exception the instructor shows.

docs.title: CML and reachability
docs.text: What you see What to check Topology stays empty CML nodes are booted. SR-PCE provider is reachable. BGP-LS from the IGP is up. Give a freshly started lab several minutes to advertise. A PE is unreachable in Network Devices The node is booted, the management address pings from the path CNC uses, and the credential profile name on the device is the lab profile. Inventory is thin or old The device has a Data Gateway mapping, and the gateway is enrolled.

docs.title: Providers and collection
docs.text: What you see What to check SR-PCE provider down Provider reachability in Administration > Manage Provider Access, then the PCE process on the CML node the instructor names. NSO provider down The same provider page. Chapter 6 waits until NSO is reachable. Link utilization is blank Data Gateway collection and SNMP credentials. LCM cannot see congestion without those counters. Link utilization is 0% Expected on an idle CML lab. Chapter 7 accepts that number.

docs.title: SR policy
docs.text: What you see What to check No PCC-initiated row The instructor's prepared policy is missing. Continue with the PCE-initiated create. Path preview is empty SR-PCE has no path in that policy type (SRv6 versus SR-MPLS). Confirm you are on the whiteboard's tab, then confirm SIDs on the topology layer. Policy is down on the headend PCEP session on the headend (show segment-routing traffic-eng pcc ipv4 peer or the IPv6 form). Color collision with another seat.

docs.title: L3VPN
docs.text: What you see What to check Dry run names another seat Close it. Reopen PTA-L3-SEAT-<seat> only. Commit fails on the profile or template The instance profile name on the whiteboard. The NSO L3VPN function pack is an instructor concern. Service out of sync NSO provider reachability, then the device sync state for your two PEs. Read sync before you debug the VRF. Overlay does not show your policy Steering color is 200 + seat, and pta-pce-seat-<seat> is still up.

docs.title: LCM
docs.text: What you see What to check No domain card SR-PCE topology and BGP-LS link-state instance-id. The instructor configures LCM once. No recommendation Compare interface utilization with the interface threshold. Below the threshold, an empty dashboard is the correct result. Many recommendations appear at once Thresholds were lowered on an idle lab. The instructor owns the dashboard. Students do not commit.

docs.title: Assistant
docs.text: What you see What to check Backend offline The instructor restarts the assistant. Students wait. Inventory tool returns an error Reachability from the MCP server to the CNC URL, and the server's credential. That credential is not entered in chat. The count disagrees with Network Devices Write both numbers. Inventory counts modules as well as chassis on some views. Confirm you are comparing the same object type.

docs.title: End of day
docs.text:
Delete in this order, and only your own objects:

  1. L3VPN PTA-L3-SEAT-<seat>
  2. PCE-initiated policy pta-pce-seat-<seat>

Leave the PCC-initiated policy, the LCM configuration, ZTP objects, templates, and providers in place.
